title: processkit-cli `doctor --json` runtime-qualification report
description: The single JSON line `processkit-cli doctor --json` prints to stdout — the side-effecting counterpart of `probe --json`. Where the probe report says what this *binary* is, this one says what this *host* did: it is written after a bounded scratch run of the binary's own harmless child, and carries the facts observed doing it (registry creation and owner-only protection, containment mechanism and abrupt-cleanup level, a local control-transport inspect/cancel/terminal round-trip, a confirmed-empty teardown, optionally the resource controller, and per-phase timings). Printed in both the qualified and the unqualified case (a failed phase or an unmet `--require-*` expectation exits HOST_UNQUALIFIED (116) with `qualified: false`), so the caller always has a parseable result. The normative prose is docs/troubleshooting.md, "Qualifying a host: `doctor`", and docs/integration.md §1; the in-code source of truth is src/doctor.rs. Validated against fixtures/schema/cli/doctor.jsonl, and against the real binary's output, by tests/machine_output.rs.

doctor_version.description: The report's own format version (src/doctor.rs, DOCTOR_VERSION) — an axis of its own, independent of the JSONL `schema_version`, `probe_version`, `snapshot_version`, `attestation_version`, `error_version`, and `registry_version`. Versioned because this report is meant to be kept: a failed qualification writes it into the diagnostics directory it leaves behind, where it is read later, out of context, by someone who did not run it (fixtures/schema/cli/README.md, "Versioning"). Pinned here: a bump is a breaking change to this shape and updates this document with it.

binary.description: The binary's package name, so a report read out of context still names what produced it.

version.description: The binary's semantic version (CARGO_PKG_VERSION) — which build performed this qualification.

os.description: The host's operating system as this build names it (`std::env::consts::OS`: `windows`, `linux`, `macos`, …). The coarsest fact about *which* host was qualified, and the first thing a reader of a kept report needs. Open-ended on purpose: it is Rust's target vocabulary, not one this project defines.

qualified.description: Whether every phase succeeded **and** every `--require-*` expectation was met. The one-line verdict; `failures` and `mismatches` are the two independent reasons it can be false, and everything else here is the evidence behind it. `false` exits HOST_UNQUALIFIED (116).

registry.description: The per-user run registry as observed, or `null` if that phase never ran.

containment.description: The containment mechanism as observed, or `null` if no scratch run ever reported one.

control.description: The local control-transport round-trip as observed, or `null` if it never got far enough to report anything.

cleanup.description: Teardown and artifact cleanup as observed, or `null` if the scratch run never reached teardown.

resource_controller.description: The optional resource-controller check, or `null` when `--check-resource-controller` was not asked for. **Null means "not checked", never "not available"** — an absent fact and a negative one are different answers, and only the flag decides which of the two this field carries.

phases.description: Each phase this invocation ran, in the order it ran them. A failed phase is the last one present — except `resource_controller`, which is isolated by design and runs after every mandatory phase has already finished.

elapsed_ms.description: Wall-clock milliseconds for the whole qualification.

failures.description: One human-readable reason per **failed phase** — what this host could not do. Always present; empty when every phase succeeded.

mismatches.description: One human-readable reason per unmet `--require-*` expectation — what this host does, that the caller needed to be otherwise. Always present; empty when none was requested or all were met. Deliberately a separate array from `failures`: "this host is broken" and "this host is not the one you asked for" are different verdicts, even though both make `qualified` false and both exit 116.

diagnostics_dir.description: The directory holding this run's scratch artifacts — the scratch run's JSONL stream, its stdout/stderr, and a copy of this report — kept **only** when a phase failed, and named here so the next step is a path rather than a guess. `null` on a host that completed every phase, which leaves nothing behind at all (including when a `--require-*` expectation was the only thing unmet: nothing failed, so there is nothing to keep).

then.description: A qualified host carries neither reason and leaves nothing behind: `qualified` is exactly `failures.is_empty() && mismatches.is_empty()` (src/doctor.rs), and the scratch directory is kept only for a failure.

else.description: An unqualified report always names at least one concrete reason, in one array or the other — never a bare negative verdict.

then.description: A failed phase always leaves the named diagnostics directory behind (src/doctor.rs, `into_report`), so the evidence and the verdict can be read together.

registryFacts.description: The per-user run registry this host resolved, and whether it really is protected to its owner alone.

dir.description: The registry directory this host resolves to (`PROCESSKIT_CLI_REGISTRY_DIR` if set, else the platform default — docs/registry.md). Named explicitly because "which directory" is the first question a permissions problem raises.

owner_only.description: Whether the directory grants access to its owner alone, **re-read from the filesystem** after the create rather than inferred from the create succeeding. The check is the very predicate the registry's own tests use (src/registry/platform/{unix,windows}.rs, `is_owner_only`): a `0700` mode compare on unix, a binary-SID ACE compare against a protected DACL on Windows. `false` fails the phase — another account on this host could read or alter the records.

protection.description: How that protection is expressed on this platform, so `owner_only` names a mechanism rather than an opinion (src/registry/mod.rs, OWNER_ONLY_PROTECTION).

containmentFacts.description: What this host actually gave the scratch run, read from that run's own `run_started` event.

mechanism.description: The containment mechanism this host selected — the same vocabulary the JSONL `run_started` event publishes (docs/schema.md; `unknown` is that event's own forward-compatible fallback for a mechanism this build predates). `--require-mechanism` compares against this value exactly.

abrupt_cleanup.description: What still reaps the tree if the runner is killed without running destructors — an OS-derived property of the mechanism, not a setting (docs/platform-support.md), and the same vocabulary `run_started` publishes. `--require-abrupt-cleanup` compares against this value exactly; the three values are platform facts and this project publishes no ordering between them, so it is not an "at least this strong" comparison.

root_pid.description: The scratch child's PID as the run reported it, or `null` if the backend exposed none. Evidence that a real process was really contained, rather than that a container was merely created.

controlFacts.description: The local control transport, driven as an ordinary client against the scratch run — the same client code `inspect` and `cancel` use, not a parallel one written to pass.

endpoint.description: The endpoint the scratch run published and this qualification connected to: a unix socket path, or a Windows named pipe name.

transport.description: Which local transport this build binds (src/control/mod.rs, TRANSPORT).

inspected_members.description: How many container members the `inspect` round-trip came back with — the round-trip's *content*, not merely its success. At least one on a healthy host (the scratch child itself); the exact number is a property of the platform's member enumeration.

cancel_acknowledged.description: Whether the runner acknowledged the `cancel` verb — the mutating half of the round-trip, which a read-only `inspect` cannot establish on its own.

terminal_exit_code.description: The exit code the scratch runner ended with, or `null` if it was ended by a signal rather than an exit. `108` (CONTROL_CANCELLED) on a healthy host: the cancel this qualification sent is what ended it.

terminal_source.description: The terminal `runner_exit` event's `source` — `control_cancel` on a healthy host — read from the run's own stream, so the run's account and this report cannot disagree. `null` when the stream carried no terminal event. Its vocabulary is fixtures/schema/v1/schema.json's `runnerExit.source`, which stays its single source of truth and is deliberately not duplicated here.

cleanupFacts.description: Teardown and artifact cleanup — the half of containment a host can fail *after* everything else worked.

members_before.description: The container's size as teardown began (`cleanup_started.members_before`), or `null` if the run reported no teardown at all.

remaining.description: Members still in the post-kill snapshot (`cleanup_finished.remaining`), or `null` if the run reported no teardown. On the `process_group` mechanism a non-zero value is **not** on its own a failed teardown: that snapshot is a `kill(pid, 0)` probe, which a just-exited child nobody has reaped yet still answers (docs/schema.md, "cleanup_finished"), so it is published as an observed fact alongside `teardown_snapshot_conclusive` — the field that says which of the two readings applies — rather than treated as a survivor. On every other mechanism it is conclusive and fails the phase.

remaining_pids.description: The PIDs behind `remaining`, when there were any. Always present; empty when there were none.

read_error.description: Whether **either** member read failed during teardown (`cleanup_started.read_error` or `cleanup_finished.read_error`). This is what makes a `remaining: 0` mean something: a zero from a failed read is a gap, not a confirmed-empty container. `true` fails the phase on every mechanism.

confirmed_empty.description: The reads succeeded **and** nothing remained. The conjunction is the point — either half alone would be an unearned claim. Reported independently of the phase verdict, which is mechanism-aware (see `remaining` and `teardown_snapshot_conclusive`).

teardown_snapshot_conclusive.description: Whether a **non-empty** post-teardown snapshot would have been conclusive evidence that something survived: `true` on every mechanism whose teardown is atomic over the whole tree, `false` on the POSIX `process_group` fallback alone. It is what distinguishes the two readings of the same `remaining` count — on that one mechanism a `confirmed_empty: false` is the honest limit of what the platform can report rather than proof of a survivor, and does not fail the qualification. Published as a field rather than left to prose because a consumer deciding what to do about a non-zero `remaining` needs it.

registry_record_removed.description: Whether the scratch run's registry record is gone. Established by polling the registry until it disappears, not assumed from the runner having exited: a runner that exits without removing its record leaves exactly the stale entry `prune` exists to reap, and a caller qualifying a host wants to know that here rather than in production.

endpoint_released.description: Whether the control endpoint was released: nothing answers a connection to it any more, and — on unix, where the transport creates a private socket directory on disk — that directory is gone too. On Windows a named pipe is a kernel object that cannot outlive its runner, so only the first half is a filesystem question there.

scratch_removed.description: Whether the scratch directory (the run's JSONL stream and the runner's stdout/stderr) was deleted. `false` exactly when it was deliberately kept as `diagnostics_dir`.

resourceControllerFacts.description: The optional whole-tree resource-controller check, present only when `--check-resource-controller` asked for it **and** the check reached a verdict. It runs as a second, separate scratch run *after* every mandatory phase has finished, so a host without a controller still gets a complete report about everything else. Every way the check could not be *performed* — no budget left, a scratch run that would not spawn, a wait that could not complete, or a scratch run that ended for some reason other than the cap — fails the `resource_controller` phase and leaves this object `null` rather than writing a negative nobody established.

requested.description: The cap this check asked for, spelled as the `run` flag that asks for it — so the report names a reproducible invocation rather than an abstraction.

available.description: Whether the container could be created with that cap installed. `false` means this host's containment mechanism cannot enforce whole-tree resource limits (docs/resource-limits.md), which is a property of the platform rather than a fault — it fails nothing by itself, and only `--require-resource-controller` turns it into a verdict. It is written **only on the scratch run's own evidence that the cap was refused**: its `limit_hit` event, under the `BACKEND` (102) code that event accompanies. A scratch run that ended any other way (a generic container-creation failure under that same code, a setup error, a deadline, a signal) establishes nothing about a resource controller, so it fails the `resource_controller` phase and leaves the whole object `null` instead — "this host cannot" and "nobody found out" are different answers.

detail.description: What the scratch run's own `limit_hit` event reported when the cap could not be installed — which limit (`memory` / `processes` / `cpu`) and the backend's own explanation. `null` exactly when the cap installed cleanly, since an `available: false` is only ever written on that event. Free text: a diagnostic, not a contract.

phaseReport.description: One phase of the qualification, and what it cost.

phase.description: The phase's name. The six mandatory phases run in the order listed; `resource_controller` is the optional seventh and runs last.

elapsed_ms.description: Wall-clock milliseconds this phase took. The reason a slow host is diagnosable rather than a generic failure: the per-phase totals say *where* the time went.

detail.description: Why it failed; `null` on a phase that succeeded. Free text: a diagnostic, not a contract — which is also why nothing else is ever put here: a fact worth acting on gets a field of its own instead of a note only a human could read. The mechanism-dependent qualification a reader might expect here is published as `cleanupFacts.teardown_snapshot_conclusive`, and a successful phase leaves this `null` even then (`tests/doctor.rs` asserts that for every phase of a qualified host).
